hook: A handful of short paragraphs and one rule, built around something you do thousands of times a day without noticing. Read it slowly and notice how little it actually explains. The fear isn't really in the description of the thing; it's in what the rule demands of the staff who have to stand in the room with it.
whyItMatters:
This is one of the best-known and highest-rated files on the wiki, and its skeleton (item number, object class, containment procedures, description) is the same one nearly every later entry uses. The flat, report-style voice that defines the whole site is already fully formed here, in a page you can read in a minute.

It also shows how much an entry can do with almost no backstory. There is no interview, no addendum, no explanation of where the statue came from, and it has still become the reference point people reach for when they explain what an SCP is.
thingsToNotice:
The core mechanic, stated plainly: the statue can only move when nobody is looking at it, and when it does move it kills, either by breaking the victim's neck just below the skull or by strangling them. That is why the procedures are written for the staff rather than the object: at least three people per entry, two of them assigned to keep their eyes on it the whole time, and a spoken warning before anyone blinks, so the horror lives in the logistics.

The last two paragraphs undercut the calm tone with concrete leftovers of what happens off-screen. Guards hear stone grinding inside the cell when it is empty, and the file treats this as routine. The reddish-brown stain on the floor turns out to be a mix of blood and excrement whose source nobody can explain, and the answer to it is simply a cleaning rota every two weeks.

Notice too what stays blank: it arrived at Site-19 in 1993, it is made of concrete and rebar with traces of Krylon paint, and its origin is unknown, a gap the article trusts you to fill yourself.
